missions/russian-orthodox-mission/name: Russian Orthodox missions (Stephen of Perm, Innocent of Alaska, Nicholas of Japan)
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/status: The tsarist missionary system collapsed after 1917, when Soviet persecution destroyed the Imperial Orthodox Missionary Society and most missions. Its daughter churches survived independently: the Orthodox Church in America (autocephalous 1970, with Alaska Native parishes), the autonomous Japanese Orthodox Church (1970), and Orthodox communities in China and Korea. After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate revived missionary work inside Russia, now closely aligned with the Russian state.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/summar: Russian Orthodox mission advanced with the expansion of Muscovy and the Russian Empire across northern Eurasia and into Alaska. At its best it continued the Cyrillo-Methodian tradition of vernacular scripture and liturgy: Stephen of Perm created an alphabet for the Komi in the fourteenth century, Nikolai Ilminsky built native-language schools for the Volga peoples, Innocent Veniaminov translated scripture into Aleut and Tlingit, and Nicholas Kasatkin founded a self-sustaining Japanese Orthodox church. It was also an arm of the state, using tax privileges, legal penalties and force to convert Muslims and animists, and was entangled with colonial exploitation in Siberia and Alaska.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/story:
The first great Russian missionary was Stephen of Perm (c. 1340–1396), a monk from Ustyug who learned the language of the Komi (Zyrians) and, in deliberate imitation of Cyril, devised the Old Permic or Abur alphabet in about 1372. From 1379 he preached on the Vychegda river, translated services into Komi and was consecrated first bishop of Perm in 1383. His Life by Epiphanius the Wise celebrates both his translations and his felling of a sacred birch and burning of idols. Monks of the northern Thebaid, inspired by Sergius of Radonezh, carried Christianity to Finnic peoples of the north; Trifon of Pechenga worked among the Sami in the sixteenth century. Stephen's alphabet fell out of use within two centuries, replaced by Church Slavonic and Russian.

When Ivan IV conquered Kazan in 1552 mission became an instrument of empire over Muslim and animist peoples. Archbishop Gurii of Kazan (1555) was instructed to win converts gently, but mosques were destroyed and baptised Tatars ('Kryashens') were given privileges. In the eighteenth century the Office for the Affairs of New Converts (1731/1740–1764) offered converts exemption from taxes and military recruitment – shifting the burden to unbaptised neighbours – while churches replaced mosques; under Bishop Luka Konashevich of Kazan hundreds of mosques were demolished, and there were mass baptisms of Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and Mordvins who often understood little of the faith. In Siberia Metropolitan Filofei Leshchinsky of Tobolsk (1702–1721) baptised tens of thousands of Khanty and Mansi, burning their sacred images. Apostasy from Orthodoxy was a criminal offence until the 1905 edict of toleration, after which tens of thousands of baptised Tatars returned openly to Islam.

The nineteenth century brought reform. Makary Glukharev founded the Altai mission in 1830, insisting on long instruction before baptism and on translation; he also began a translation of the Old Testament into modern Russian. Nikolai Ilminsky (1822–1891), a Kazan orientalist, developed a system of schools teaching in the mother tongues of the Volga peoples using Cyrillic alphabets, with native teachers and clergy trained at the Kazan Central Baptised-Tatar School (1863) and Teachers' Seminary (1872). Ilminsky's aim was to bind non-Russians to Orthodoxy and the empire before Islam or nationalism could claim them; Russian nationalists attacked it for slowing Russification, and Tatar Muslims for its proselytism, but it gave Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and others their first literature. The Imperial Orthodox Missionary Society was founded in 1870 under Metropolitan Innocent.

In 1794 eight monks from Valaam reached Kodiak in Russian America at the invitation of the merchant Grigory Shelikhov, whose company had massacred Alutiiq people at Awa'uq (Refuge Rock) in 1784. The monks protested the Russian-American Company's abuse of Native hunters and hostages; Hieromonk Juvenaly was killed around 1796, and the monk Herman lived on Spruce Island until 1837, defending Aleuts and running an orphanage. The priest Ioann Veniaminov arrived at Unalaska in 1824, built a church with Aleut labour, devised an Aleut alphabet with the chief Ivan Pankov and wrote the first Aleut book, Indication of the Way into the Kingdom of Heaven (1833, printed 1840). At Sitka from 1834 he learned Tlingit, and in 1840, as the widowed monk Innocent, he became bishop of Kamchatka, the Kurils and the Aleutians, later serving as metropolitan of Moscow (1868–1879). Orthodoxy took deep root among Aleuts, Alutiiq and Yupik, partly because clergy and Native readers ran schools in Native languages. After the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867, American policy under the Presbyterian Sheldon Jackson suppressed Native languages in schools, while the Orthodox church remained a refuge of Native identity.

In Japan, Ivan Kasatkin (Nicholas) arrived at Hakodate in 1861 as chaplain to the Russian consulate, studied Japanese language and literature for years, and baptised his first converts, including the former samurai and Shinto priest Sawabe Takuma, secretly in 1868, while Christianity was still banned. Moving to Tokyo in 1872, he relied on Japanese catechists and clergy, translated the liturgy and New Testament with Nakai Tsugumaro, and built the Cathedral of the Resurrection (Nikolai-dō, 1891). During the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) he remained in Japan, praying for its people while ministering to Russian prisoners. At his death in 1912 the church numbered about 33,000. A Russian Ecclesiastical Mission had existed in Beijing since 1715, serving the descendants of Albazin Cossacks and acting as an informal embassy; during the Boxer uprising of 1900 some 222 Chinese Orthodox were killed. A Korean mission opened in 1900.

The revolution of 1917 ended this era. The Soviet state closed missions, executed or imprisoned clergy and cut off overseas dioceses, which reorganised as the Metropolia in North America (later the Orthodox Church in America), the Japanese church and the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia. After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate rebuilt dioceses, translated scripture into minority languages and created a Synodal Missionary Department (1995), while supporting the 1997 law restricting 'non-traditional' religions and opposing Western Protestant mission in Russia as proselytism. Its close alignment with the state, including support for the war in Ukraine framed by 'Russian world' ideology, has been sharply criticised by other Orthodox theologians.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/belief: Eastern Orthodox faith and worship as the fullness of Christianity, with the Byzantine-Slavonic liturgy at the centre of mission.
The Cyrillo-Methodian principle that peoples should worship in their own language, revived by Stephen of Perm, Ilminsky, Innocent and Nicholas.
Symphony of church and state: the tsar as protector of Orthodoxy and conversion as integration into the Russian realm.
Baptism as entry into both the church and imperial society, with apostasy treated as a crime until 1905.
Monastic holiness and the 'elder' tradition as the source of missionary vocation (Sergius of Radonezh, Valaam, Optina).
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/strate: Creation of alphabets and translations: Old Permic for Komi, Cyrillic scripts for Volga and Siberian languages, Aleut and Tlingit writing.
State incentives for converts – tax and conscription exemptions – and penalties for apostasy and for proselytising by other faiths.
Destruction of sacred groves, idols and mosques and their replacement with churches.
Native-language schools and the training of indigenous teachers and priests (Ilminsky system, Alaskan readers, Japanese catechists).
Missions attached to trading companies and military outposts (Russian-American Company, Siberian forts).
Monastic settlements as centres of instruction and charity, such as Herman's Spruce Island and Glukharev's Altai mission.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/groups: Komi (Zyrians) and other Finnic peoples of the Russian north.
Volga Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and Mordvins after the conquest of Kazan.
Khanty, Mansi, Yakut (Sakha), Buryat and Altaian peoples of Siberia.
Aleuts, Alutiiq, Yupik and Tlingit of Alaska.
Japanese, especially in Hakodate, Tokyo and northern Honshu.
Albazinian descendants and some Han Chinese in Beijing; Koreans after 1900.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/challe: Resistance of Muslim Tatars and Bashkirs, and widespread return to Islam or traditional religion after nominal baptism.
Huge distances and shortage of clergy who knew local languages.
Conflict between missionary ideals and state or commercial interests (Russian-American Company, settlers).
Russian nationalist opposition to non-Russian-language liturgy.
After 1867 in Alaska, competition with American Protestant missions and English-only schooling.
Soviet persecution after 1917, which destroyed most missionary institutions.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/harms/: Conversion was frequently coerced or bought: tax and conscription exemptions for converts, criminal penalties for apostasy and pressure on whole villages produced nominal Christians.
Hundreds of mosques in the Kazan region were destroyed in the 1740s, and Muslim Tatars faced restrictions designed to promote conversion.
Sacred sites, images and groves of Komi, Khanty, Mansi and other peoples were burned or cut down by missionaries, from Stephen of Perm to Filofei of Tobolsk.
Mission in Alaska depended on the Russian-American Company, which exploited Aleut and Alutiiq hunters through forced labour and hostage-taking.
Missions often served Russification and imperial control, even when using native languages.
In the post-Soviet period the church has supported legal restrictions on other religions and aligned itself with state nationalism and the war against Ukraine.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/develo: First alphabets and books for many peoples of Russia and Alaska, including Komi, Aleut, Chuvash and Mari.
A self-governing Japanese Orthodox Church with Japanese clergy and liturgy.
Orthodoxy as a lasting element of Alaska Native identity, and the Orthodox Church in America.
Ilminsky's mother-tongue schooling, which shaped later Soviet language policy and national literatures.
Saints – Stephen of Perm, Herman and Innocent of Alaska, Nicholas of Japan – who model a respectful, linguistically engaged mission within Orthodoxy.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/outcom: Russian Orthodox mission made Orthodoxy the faith of many Finnic, Volga, Siberian and Alaskan peoples and planted lasting churches in Japan and North America, but its dependence on imperial power meant that many conversions were nominal and that Islam and indigenous religions revived whenever coercion lifted. Its most enduring fruits came where missionaries translated, educated and handed leadership to local Christians.

missions/russian-orthodox-mission/journe: Stephen of Perm's mission to the Komi
Stephen travelled up the Vychegda to found churches among the Komi, went to Moscow to be consecrated bishop in 1383 and returned to his see at Ust-Vym.
Archimandrite Joasaph, Herman, Juvenaly and companions
A journey of some 12,000 km across Siberia and the North Pacific; the monks arrived at Kodiak in September 1794.
Ioann Veniaminov to Unalaska and Sitka
Ioann Veniaminov (St Innocent) and his family
Ten years at Unalaska among the Aleuts, then Sitka among the Tlingit; after his wife's death he became a monk and returned to Sitka as bishop in 1841.
Crossing Siberia overland, Kasatkin reached Hakodate in July 1861 and moved to Tokyo in 1872, where he founded the mission headquarters at Surugadai.
The Russian Ecclesiastical Mission to Beijing
Sent by Peter the Great with Kangxi's consent to serve the Albazinian community, the mission also functioned as Russia's diplomatic and scholarly presence in China until 1860.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/agreem: Stephen of Perm, Ilminsky and Innocent all explicitly invoked Cyril and Methodius in creating alphabets and vernacular liturgy.
Shared commitment to scripture in minority languages; the Russian Bible Society (1812–1826) translated into several languages of the empire before Orthodox opposition closed it.
The Russian Orthodox Church joined the World Council of Churches in 1961, and Orthodox theologians contributed to ecumenical mission thought on liturgy and witness.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/disagr: After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate condemned Western evangelical missions in Russia as 'proselytism' on canonical Orthodox territory and backed the 1997 law restricting them.
Pentecostal and charismatic churches growing in Russia and Ukraine are treated by the Patriarchate as sects, and have faced legal restrictions and harassment.
missions/russian-orthodox-mission/deviat: The Cyrillo-Methodian ideal of persuasion in one's own tongue was repeatedly displaced by state-backed coercion and material inducements.
Mission became tied to Russification and imperial expansion, at odds with Orthodoxy's own teaching that the church transcends nations (condemned as 'phyletism' in 1872).
Recent alignment of the Moscow Patriarchate with state ideology has been criticised by Orthodox theologians in the 2022 Declaration on the 'Russian World' teaching.
